newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW - RGC sees no Peru equity raising. [CORRECTED 11:47 GMT]
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - RGC sees no Peru equity raising. [CORRECTED 11:47 GMT]

text.p: Mineral sands and metals miner RGC Ltd assured shareholder on Tuesday that plans to buy and develop a US$300 million gold/copper project in Peru would not require any equity raising.

Earlier, RGC announced it had agreed to buy the Cerro Corona project in the Andes in Northern Peru for a US$2 million deposit and a one-off payment of US$34 million after due diligence or US$37 million in three payments over three years.
RGC bought the mine from the privately-owned family company Grupo Gubbins.
RGC Managing Director Mark Bethwaite told Reuters in an interview he could not say how much would have to be invested in this specific project.
"But similar projects of this nature around the world are in the US$250 million to US$350 million range," Bethwaite said.
"RGC has a very strong balance sheet and there is absolutely no thought of any equity raising for this," he said.
Cerro Corona is a copper/gold deposit at an altitude of 3,500 metres about 600 km (375 miles) north Lima and 90 km (56 miles) north of the city of Cajamarca.
The region includes the Yanacocha gold mine, Minero Peru's Michiquillay copper/gold property and Cambior's La Granja copper project.
Cerro Corona is estimated to contain total measured, indicated, inferred and potential resources of 378,956,000 tonnes of sulphide ore with 0.465 grams per tonne of gold and 0.291 percent copper.
The estimates were made from 46,000 metres of drilling. (Corrects ore tonnage and copper ratio)
RGC said it planned to develop a large open pit mine processing 35,000 tonnes per day of sulphide ore to produce a copper/gold concentrate.

The mine had a life on present sulphide ores of at least 12 years followed by oxide ore processing and was expected to produce about 52,000 tonnes of copper concentrate and 230,000 ounces of gold annualy.
Bethwaite defended RGC's decision to buy the Peruvian project, which had been abandoned by Barrick Gold Corp last year.

Barrick had carried out the drilling work on the project and had an option to buy it from the Gubbins family. But it decided in October 1996 to pull out, relinquish the option and take a C$38 million charge to offset the exploration costs.
Barrick's withdrawal was linked to two factors specific to the Canadian gold mining group, Bethwaite said.
"Firstly, it's predominantly a copper project and they're a gold company, and secondly, they were faced with a very high options exercise payout," he said.
Bethwaite said he could not say how high Barrick's options exercise payout was, suffice to say it was higher than what RGC would pay.
Bethwaite said he acknowledged perceptions about country risk in places like Peru, but that RGC had to look in places like Latin America to find such projects.
"Whilst there is clearly an issue about moving offshore, this is where projects are being discovered, and more importantly, being developed," he said.

"There's no question that most Australian mining companies would like to find these sorts of projects in Australia, but the reality is the hit rate in Australia is far less than in South America, which is a major emerging base metals Province.
"And, once you have found it in Australia, it is subject to interminable delays and I cite Century Zinc there."
"We see the whole of South America as being on an improving trend (in country risk terms). Peru we feel is a good environment in which to do business in," he said.
RGC's shares closed 15 cents lower at A$4.10 on Tuesday.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
